Adolescent fertility rates (ages 15–24) are displayed for six bins of youth labor force participation. Each boxplot summarizes the distribution of fertility rates within its bin, while the color of each box reflects the median female-to-male literacy ratio for that labor-force-participation range.

</figcaption>

</figure>

The visualization illustrates adolescent fertility rates (for females ages 15-24) for six bins of youth labor force participation in order to reveal important connections and relationships between labor, education, and reproductive behavior. Each boxplot summarizes the distribution of fertility rates within its bin. The color of each box reflects the median female-to-make literacy ratio for that specific labor-force-participation range. 

In the lowest labor force participation bin, adolescents demonstrate both the lowest average fertility rates and the lowest female-to-male literacy ratios. This suggests that entering and engaging in the workforce may be caused by restricted access to schooling that can thus suppress literacy and childbearing in adolescents. Additionally, entering certain forms of work may not require or encourage formal schooling which can further enforce poor literacy outcomes. 

As labor force participation increases, average fertility rates increase slightly, but fertility outcomes vary the most particularly in the 33.5–40.4 participation bin. This displays the greatest variability and can indicate that adolescents who enter the workforce at higher rates might be doing so at ages that experience close to or peak fertility years. The visualization illustrates that the highest labor force participation groups also happen to contain some of the highest fertility values. This goes against the idea that greater economic stability leads to delayed fertility amongst adolescent females. Instead, the visualization suggests that high adolescent labor participation may lead to early work and parenthood. 

This data spotlights the importance of addressing adolescent labor patterns with respect to their social and economic environments instead of assuming that they are the same as adult labor fertility patterns.
